headline: You plan first, test first, and keep payments correct.

archetype.name: The Ledger Guardian
archetype.description: You treat every change to money-moving code as a risk to plan for. You want plans, tests and rollbacks in place before any code changes.

dimensions.title: Plan, test, then step
dimensions.summary: You usually ask for a plan, hypotheses or competing approaches before any code. Then you work in small steps, write tests first and limit what the AI may touch.

evidence.quote: Before writing any code, outline a plan for adding idempotency keys to the payments API. List the risks.
Keep it under 80 lines and add tests first.
Do not touch the handlers yet.
refactor in small commits, one concern per commit, and tell me the commit messages first.

dimensions.title: Short, polite, decisive
dimensions.summary: Your prompts are brief imperatives. You often ask the AI to explain why before it changes anything, then state your decision in a few words.

evidence.quote: Can you explain why before changing anything?
Agreed, use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.
Let's keep the mutex.

dimensions.title: Go and Postgres depth
dimensions.summary: You work on Go billing and ledger services and know PostgreSQL well: isolation levels, deferred constraint triggers and row locking. Your tools include sqlc, testcontainers and rapid, and you avoid ORMs.

evidence.quote: Explain how this behaves under READ COMMITTED versus SERIALIZABLE.
Use a deferred constraint trigger. Write the SQL and property-based tests with rapid.
Please don't use an ORM here, plain sqlc queries.

dimensions.title: Correctness and production readiness
dimensions.summary: You keep coming back to idempotency, race conditions, delivery guarantees and zero-downtime operations. You also want decisions written down in ADRs, design docs and runbooks.

evidence.quote: exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery and how consumers should deduplicate
rotate the database credentials without downtime
Document the decision in an ADR.
Add alerting thresholds and explain how you chose them.

dimensions.title: Front-load the requirements
dimensions.summary: Your workflow is already disciplined. The next step is to put the constraints you add in follow-ups (sections, edge cases, no ORM) into the first request.

evidence.quote: The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Run through the edge cases again: leap years, currency rounding, negative line items.

traits.name: Plan before code
traits.description: In most sessions you ask for a plan, hypotheses or a comparison of approaches before any implementation.

evidence.quote: Before writing any code, outline a plan for adding idempotency keys to the payments API. List the risks.
Propose two approaches and compare them.
Help me form hypotheses before we look at code.
Now break the rollout into PR-sized steps.

traits.name: Test-first verifier
traits.description: You often ask for tests first, characterization tests, property tests or benchmarks, so you have proof the code works.

evidence.quote: Keep it under 80 lines and add tests first.
Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.
Add a benchmark so we can compare later.

traits.name: Tight scope keeper
traits.description: You often limit what the AI may touch and ask for small outputs such as a single step or just the diff.

evidence.quote: Do not touch the handlers yet.
Show me the diff only.
Let's start with step 1 only

traits.name: Reasoning on demand
traits.description: You often ask the AI to justify its reasoning before you accept a change.

evidence.quote: Can you explain why before changing anything?
Review this Go function for race conditions. Explain your reasoning step by step.
explain how you chose them.

traits.name: Documentation minded
traits.description: You regularly ask for ADRs, structured design docs and runbooks with rollback sections.

evidence.quote: Document the decision in an ADR.
Sections: context, goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, rollout.
a verification step after each stage and a rollback section

funFacts: None of your 36 prompts were sent on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday.
26 of your prompts landed in the 9:00 and 10:00 hours.
Your correction rate is 0%: you never had to push back on the AI.
Your median prompt is just 85 characters long.

improvements.title: Put requirements in the first request
improvements.pattern: Sometimes you add key requirements, like the runbook's required sections or the edge cases to cover, in a follow-up prompt.
improvements.impact: Extra prompts went to adding sections and re-checking edge cases that could have been covered in the first output.
improvements.suggestion: When you already know the structure or the edge cases, list them in the first request. Your follow-ups can then be about refining the output, not completing the spec.

evidence.quote: Write a runbook in docs/runbooks/rotate-db-creds.md.
The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Run through the edge cases again: leap years, currency rounding, negative line items.

rewrite.after: Write a runbook in docs/runbooks/rotate-db-creds.md. Include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.

improvements.title: Name the code under review
improvements.pattern: In one session you asked for a review of "this Go function" without naming the file or the function.
improvements.impact: The AI has to guess which code you mean, which can lead to a review of the wrong function.
improvements.suggestion: Give the file path and function name, or paste the code, in the review request.

evidence.quote: Review this Go function for race conditions.

improvements.title: State the audience and format
improvements.pattern: Once, you asked for a changelog summary without saying who would read it or what format to use.
improvements.impact: Without an audience, the summary's tone and level of detail are left to the AI.
improvements.suggestion: Add one line saying who the summary is for and what format to use, for example a single bullet for API consumers.

evidence.quote: Write a short summary for the changelog.
